overview: British Guiana was formed in 1831 by joining British-controlled Demerara-Essequibo and Berbice, in present-day Guyana. Its earlier history involved Dutch colonies. The imported 1783 to 1914 dates are not the colony’s lifespan, and the associated outline chiefly covers neighbouring Suriname, so it is not an accurate map of this colony.

periods.title: British control before unification
periods.summary: The British retained important Dutch institutions after taking possession in 1803.

periods.title: Union and emancipation
periods.summary: The united colony entered emancipation through a coercive apprenticeship period, which ended in 1838.

periods.title: Colonial society and political change
periods.summary: Formerly enslaved people built new communities while indentured migration brought further workers and families.

items.text: Britain kept the Dutch-origin Court of Policy after taking control. British Guiana’s political institutions therefore combined successive colonial inheritances. The 1831 union created one colony from administrations whose settlement and governing structures were already much older.

The 1834 abolition legislation did not immediately end compulsory work for everyone. Under “apprenticeship,” many people still owed unpaid labour to former enslavers for most of the working week. Full emancipation in the colony followed on 1 August 1838.

Resistance continued during that transition. In August 1834, Damon led an uprising on the Essequibo coast against the new labour arrangements. Colonial forces suppressed it and executed him. People subjected to plantation rule actively challenged what officials called a gradual path to freedom.

In 1839, eighty-three formerly enslaved people pooled money to buy Plantation Northbrook, later called Victoria. They paid 30,000 guilders. This collective purchase gave families a place to build a community beyond the plantation labour system, a concrete achievement after emancipation.

Indian indentured migration brought another major population to the colony. Guyana’s surviving registers cover arrivals from 1838 to 1917. Their personal details help descendants recover family histories from a labour system designed to supply cheap contracted workers.

sections.title: Canals, neighbourhoods and Indigenous food technology

items.text: Georgetown’s layout still records its plantation origins. Canals once divided long plantation strips running away from the river, while a connecting raised street linked settlements and military grounds. Urban geography can preserve an older agricultural plan beneath later buildings.

Former plantations became neighbourhoods through a grid of streets. Some canals survived, while those on Church Street and Hadfield Street were filled in during the early twentieth century to make more space. A growing city reshaped the waterways inherited from its past.

An Akawaio cassava press collected near the Essequibo River in 1913 to 1916 survives in the Smithsonian. Its plaited plant-fibre tube illustrates a clever basketry principle: stretching the tube narrows it, squeezing the grated root inside. Skilled weaving created a working food-processing machine.

A Guyanese cassava sieve dated around 1910 uses cane, wood, cordage and dye. Such tools separated coarse pieces from prepared meal. The museum attributes this example only tentatively to a Carib community; its careful weaving nevertheless preserves an individual maker’s practical skill.

When imported stamps ran short in 1856, Georgetown’s newspaper printers produced an emergency supply. One-cent stamps served newspaper postage and four-cent stamps domestic letters. Clerks initialled the locally printed stamps to discourage forgery: a handwritten safeguard on a mass-produced object.

In 1873, twelve-year-old Vernon Vaughan found an 1856 one-cent stamp among his uncle’s papers. That surviving scrap became famous among collectors. An ordinary postal object, spotted by a child, preserves evidence of the colony’s printers, currency and communications.

The stamp carries the Latin motto “Damus Petimus Que Vicissim.” Translation: “We give and we ask in return.” The Smithsonian’s infrared-image description records the wording, normally difficult to read against the dark magenta paper. It is an authentic printed colonial sample.

ending.text: British Guiana became independent Guyana on 26 May 1966. The imported endpoint of 1914 does not mark the end of British rule. This card describes the historical colony named by the record; its mismatched map polygon must not be treated as an accurate boundary.
